title: The Merger
logline: Meridian buys Brightcart, and Marcus must merge two platforms, two teams and two ways of working while Brightcart's architect, Viktor Hale, competes for the same job.

modules.logline: Marcus inherits Brightcart's Scala, JVM and Kubernetes estate and must learn to read it before he can judge it.
scenes: Launch night ends at 4 a.m.: traffic fails over to the second region and Lena closes the incident. At nine, Asha announces Meridian is buying Brightcart. Viktor Hale's estate runs on the JVM. Why should a Python engineer care?

Viktor shares a repository and says nothing. Marcus opens it: case classes, Options, pattern matches, a for-comprehension over Futures. Lena says it looks like Python wearing armour. Can Marcus read Scala well enough to review it by Friday?

Brightcart's nightly fare job is a Spark Scala pipeline of typed Datasets and a few UDFs. Viktor calls it faster than anything Meridian runs. Marcus spots a map over every row. Is it really faster, or just harder to read?

At 2 a.m. the Brightcart fare job dies with an OutOfMemoryError. Lena, now leading on-call, pages Marcus. The executor heap looks fine, yet the container was killed anyway. Two kinds of out-of-memory, one alert. Which one is this?

Brightcart runs Spark and Flink for forty teams on one shared Kubernetes cluster. Pods sit Pending all morning while one team's job hogs the nodes. Viktor shrugs: requests and limits are the teams' problem. Are they, on a platform?

In a corner of Brightcart's estate sits a Hadoop cluster: YARN queues, Hive tables, eight years of ride history. Viktor wants it gone in a quarter. Dev wants it left alone. What does a safe migration off Hadoop look like?
teasers: Viktor sends Marcus a Scala repository with no comment and a Friday deadline.
Brightcart's fare job runs in Scala, and Viktor says Python could never keep up.
A 2 a.m. page: the JVM runs out of memory, but not where anyone looks.
Forty teams, one Kubernetes cluster, and pods that will not schedule.
Hidden in Brightcart's estate: a Hadoop cluster holding eight years of ride history.
Brightcart runs Databricks, Meridian runs Snowflake, and the board wants one set of tables.
modules.boss: Saturday's review: the Brightcart fare job that died at 2 a.m. Viktor blames Meridian's data volume; Marcus suspects off-heap memory. Lena chairs. Read the Scala, the GC logs and the pod events, then decide who is right.
modules.finale: Marcus approves Viktor's pull request with three comments, all correct. Viktor replies with one word: fair. Grace says, 'Learn their stack before you judge it.' Then finance asks why the same trips table exists twice, in Databricks and Snowflake.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "What did you build today?" Marcus: "Nothing new; I learned to read another team's language so I can help the people who wrote in it."

modules.logline: Brightcart's Databricks and Meridian's Snowflake must serve one set of tables, and one rider's deletion request tests whether either can.
scenes: Merger day thirty. Brightcart's analysts live in Databricks notebooks; Meridian's finance team lives in Snowflake. Mei finds both platforms storing the same trips and billing for both. Tomas asks why there are two. Is either team wrong?

Viktor walks Marcus through a Delta table: Parquet files, a _delta_log of JSON commits, a checkpoint every ten. One query scans four thousand tiny files. How does Delta decide which files to skip, and why is it skipping so few?

Marcus returns the favour in Snowflake: micro-partitions, clustering, a warehouse that suspends after sixty seconds. Viktor's query runs in eight seconds here, but bills credits by the second. Which engine prunes better, and which is cheaper per answer?

Asha wants one copy of trips, readable from both engines. Viktor proposes Delta with UniForm; Marcus suggests Iceberg tables that Snowflake can read. Both plans dodge the same question. Who owns the writes when two engines share one table?

A rider in Bengaluru emails support: delete my data, everywhere. Her trips live in Delta, in Snowflake and in three old snapshots. Legal gives thirty days. Deleting a row is easy. How does Marcus prove it is gone from history too?

Brightcart tags support tickets with a language model inside a nightly batch job. It is cheap until a failure makes it retry every row. Viktor wants it in Snowflake next. Should a model sit inside a pipeline, and on which platform?
teasers: Viktor opens a Delta table's log and shows Marcus how it really works.
Marcus answers with Snowflake micro-partitions and the same query, timed on both.
Asha wants one copy of the trips table, read by two engines.
A rider asks to be deleted from everywhere, and legal starts a thirty-day clock.
A language model in a batch pipeline bills for every retry, row by row.
Overnight, 12% of Brightcart's trip rows disappear, and every job shows green.
modules.boss: The weekend review: the rider deletion. Support says it is done; an auditor finds her trips in a Delta time-travel version and a Snowflake clone. Walk through vacuum, retention, clones and masking, and show where the process leaked.
modules.finale: One trips table, two engines, and a deletion runbook legal signs. Viktor admits Snowflake's pruning surprised him. Grace says, 'Two tools is fine; two truths is not.' Then on Monday the trip count drops 12% overnight.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why do you need two computers to hold the same toys?" Marcus: "We don't; we are teaching both of them to share one toy box."

modules.logline: When 12% of rows vanish without a single failed job, Marcus and Lena build tests, contracts and write-audit-publish so failures can no longer hide.
scenes: Monday standup. Every Airflow task is green, yet the Brightcart trips table holds 12% fewer rows than on Friday. Tomas's dashboard already shows a dip in Chennai demand. Nothing failed. How does a pipeline lose data while reporting success?

Lena traces the loss to an inner join against a driver table that arrived late. No test checked row counts. Viktor says Brightcart tests in production. Marcus asks which tests would have caught this, and where they should run.

The driver table belongs to a Brightcart partner team, who renamed a column last Thursday without telling anyone. Viktor calls it their right. Marcus calls it a broken promise. What would a data contract between the teams actually say?

Dev proposes a rule: no table is published until it is audited. Viktor worries it doubles storage and slows every job. Marcus sketches write, audit, publish on a staging branch. Can bad data wait there without consumers noticing the delay?

Asha asks for one health dashboard: freshness, volume, schema and distribution. Lena adds CI that runs the tests on every pull request. Then a harmless rename passes CI and breaks a Snowflake view. What did the checks not see?

At 3 a.m. Lena runs an incident herself, calm, with a clear timeline in Slack. Afterwards she asks Marcus for an on-call agent that reads Airflow failures and gathers evidence. How much should an agent diagnose before a human looks?
teasers: Lena finds the missing rows behind a join that nobody tested.
A partner team renamed a column last Thursday and told nobody.
Dev wants no table published until it passes an audit.
A health dashboard stays green while a Snowflake view quietly breaks.
Lena leads a 3 a.m. incident alone, then asks for an agent.
Asha asks Marcus to design for ten times the traffic, and a lost region.
modules.boss: The weekend review: 12% of rows vanished and nobody was paged. Lena presents the timeline. Find the root cause, the missing contract, the test that should exist, and where write-audit-publish would have stopped the bad load.
modules.finale: The contract is signed, the audit step blocks bad loads, and Lena's postmortem is the clearest Marcus has read. Viktor copies it for Brightcart. Grace says, 'Make the failure loud before you make it rare.' Then Asha books a design review.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "How do you know all the toys are there?" Marcus: "We count them before anyone plays, and if some are missing, the box stays shut."

modules.logline: Asha asks for a design that survives ten times the traffic and a lost region, and Marcus and Viktor must design it out loud together.
scenes: Asha books a design review: the combined company expects ten times the trips within two years. Marcus and Viktor each get forty-five minutes at the whiteboard. Viktor starts drawing at once. Marcus starts with questions. Which approach does the room trust?

Marcus does the arithmetic aloud: two hundred million events a day, about two thousand a second, peaks ten times higher on festival nights. Mei asks what a year of storage costs. Do his numbers hold up under her questions?

The rider app needs a trip's fare in under fifty milliseconds. Viktor proposes reading straight from Delta. Dev suggests a key-value store. Kofi wants Snowflake. Three serving stores, one latency budget. Which one fits the access pattern?

Viktor asks what happens when two regions accept the same payment update. Marcus reaches for quorum, idempotency keys and exactly-once. Lena asks which of those words actually stops a double charge. Can Marcus explain it plainly?

Asha calls a surprise drill: the primary region is gone, now. Traffic doubles elsewhere, Kafka lag climbs, warehouse loads stall. Marcus and Viktor share one whiteboard and ten minutes. What fails first, and what do they shed?

Lena brings a pipeline an AI assistant wrote for the drill: tidy, documented, and wrong in two places. Viktor finds one, Marcus the other. What mistakes does AI-written pipeline code make, and how should a reviewer hunt for them?
teasers: Marcus estimates ten times scale aloud, and Mei asks what a year costs.
Three teams, three serving stores, and a fifty-millisecond budget for one fare.
Two regions accept the same payment, and Lena wants plain words.
Asha switches off a region mid-review and starts a ten-minute clock.
An AI-written pipeline looks perfect, and is wrong in two places.
Viktor proposes that every Brightcart domain team owns its own data, and Kofi objects.
modules.boss: The weekend round: the lost-region drill, replayed. Ten times the traffic, one region dark, Kafka lag rising. Clarify, estimate, draw, go deep, break it and scale it, in forty-five minutes, as Marcus and Viktor did.
modules.finale: The drill ends with no lost payments and a one-page design both names sign. Asha calls it the first document from the merged team. Grace says, 'Draw the failure first.' Then Viktor sends a memo proposing data mesh for everyone.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "What if the big computer room loses power?" Marcus: "Another room in another city takes over, and we practise that before it ever happens."

modules.logline: Viktor's push for data mesh forces Marcus to decide which domains should own their data products and which still need a central team.
scenes: Viktor's memo lands in every inbox: dissolve the central data team and give each domain its own data. Kofi's analysts worry. Dev calls it a reorganisation dressed as architecture. Why does data mesh exist, and what problem does it solve?

Asha asks for one example before any reorganisation. Marcus picks the trips dataset: an owner, a contract, SLOs, a catalogue entry, a stable interface. Lena asks what makes it a product rather than a table with a nice name.

The payments domain refuses: two engineers, no data skills, a quarter-end audit coming. Viktor says ownership is non-negotiable. Marcus suspects mesh is the wrong answer for some teams. How does he decide which domains are ready?

If every domain builds its own pipelines, who runs storage, access and quality checks? Marcus sketches a self-serve platform; Viktor adds policies enforced as code. Dev asks who wins when a domain's rule conflicts with the central one.

The trips product launches. Three weeks later, two teams use it and five still query the old warehouse copy. Kofi will not switch until it matches his numbers. How do you move consumers off a central warehouse without breaking them?

Viktor shows Brightcart's earlier mesh attempt: forty data products, eleven owners who have left, nine with no consumers. He wants it done properly this time. Marcus asks which failure modes companies hit, and which ones they are already repeating.
teasers: Asha wants one real data product before anyone reorganises anything.
The payments team refuses to own their data, and Viktor will not budge.
Domains want independence, and Dev wants to know who sets the rules.
The new trips product is live, and Kofi still queries the old copy.
Viktor opens Brightcart's graveyard of forty abandoned data products.
Dev's new pipeline template has been live six weeks, and no team uses it.
modules.boss: The weekend review: Viktor's mesh proposal, as Asha will hear it on Monday. Name which domains own data products, write one product spec with an owner, a contract and an SLO, and say where mesh is the wrong answer.
modules.finale: Three domains own products; payments stays central for now. Viktor calls it half a mesh. Marcus calls it the half that works. Grace says, 'Move ownership only where someone wants it.' Then Dev's new template sits unused.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Who owns the toys?" Marcus: "Whoever plays with them most looks after them, and promises to keep them tidy for everyone else."

modules.logline: Dev's pipeline templates sit unused until Marcus and Viktor learn to build golden paths that teams choose rather than obey.
scenes: Dev's pipeline template has been live six weeks with zero users. Brightcart teams copy Viktor's old Scala scaffold instead. Dev wants to mandate the template. Marcus wants to know why nobody chose it. What is a golden path, really?

Marcus lists how teams actually ship: a new batch pipeline, a data product, a backfill, a stream. Lena times each one: eleven days for a new pipeline. Viktor says pave everything. Which journey should they pave first?

Lena drafts the template: Airflow DAG, dbt models, tests, owner tag, alerts and cost labels, all on by default. Viktor asks how a team escapes when it needs something different. What belongs in a template, and what stays optional?

Two months later, thirty pipelines built from the template run three different versions of it. A security fix reaches only nine. Dev sighs that templates always rot. How do you keep a template alive after teams copy it?

Kofi's team wants to skip platform review, which takes a week. Viktor proposes a developer portal with one-click creation. Marcus proposes CI checks instead of the review meeting. Can guardrails replace a gate without letting risk through?

Asha asks whether the golden path works. Dev shows downloads. Marcus shows time to first pipeline, down from eleven days to one. Viktor shows the teams that left it. Which number proves teams actually chose the road?
teasers: Lena times how long a new pipeline really takes: eleven days.
The first template ships, and Viktor asks where the exit is.
Thirty pipelines, three template versions, and a security fix that reaches nine.
Kofi wants to skip the weekly platform review, and Marcus agrees with him.
Asha asks for one number that proves the golden path works.
A dashboard shows rider phone numbers to four hundred people who never needed them.
modules.boss: The weekend review: nobody uses our templates. Decide which journey to pave, what the template sets by default, how it stays current, which checks move into CI, and which metric shows teams chose it.
modules.finale: Nine of twelve new pipelines now start from the path, and Viktor's team ships one too. Grace says, 'Make the right way the easy way.' Then Lena finds rider phone numbers in a dashboard four hundred people can open.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why don't people just do it your way?" Marcus: "Because we made our way the easiest one, so now most of them want to."

modules.logline: Rider phone numbers in an open dashboard push Marcus to build governance that protects riders without slowing the teams that need the data.
scenes: Four hundred people can see rider phone numbers in a Brightcart dashboard. Nobody has misused them. Legal wants every dashboard locked. Kofi says locking everything stops the business. What is governance for, if not for saying no?

Marcus asks how many columns hold personal data. Nobody knows: names, emails, drop-off coordinates, a free-text notes field. Viktor suggests tagging by hand. Lena counts eleven thousand columns. Can classification run automatically, and how accurate must it be?

Support needs a rider's phone number for an open ticket, in their own city only. Roles alone would mean forty new roles. Viktor proposes attributes and row rules. How do roles, attributes and policies combine without becoming unmanageable?

Data scientists need to join trips to riders without seeing who the riders are. Masking breaks the join; Viktor suggests tokenisation; legal asks about pseudonymisation. Three words that sound alike. Which one protects riders and keeps the join?

A column tagged personal in Snowflake loses its tag after one Delta transform. Meanwhile legal puts a hold on Chennai trips that retention rules want deleted. Which rule wins, and how does lineage carry a tag downstream?

The auditors arrive on Monday and ask for evidence: who accessed rider data, under which policy, approved by whom. Viktor's team keeps policies in a wiki. Marcus keeps them in code. Which one survives an audit?
teasers: Lena counts eleven thousand columns, and nobody knows which hold personal data.
Support needs one phone number, and roles alone would need forty new roles.
Data scientists need to join riders to trips without knowing who they are.
A personal-data tag vanishes after one transform, and legal places a hold.
The auditors arrive on Monday, and Brightcart's access policies live in a wiki.
Asha asks a simple question nobody can answer: what does the platform team do?
modules.boss: The weekend review: the phone-number dashboard. Show how the column escaped classification, which policy should have masked it, how lineage would have carried the tag, and what evidence you would hand the auditors.
modules.finale: The audit closes with no findings, and teams barely notice the new rules. Viktor moves Brightcart's wiki into code without being asked. Grace says, 'Good governance is the kind people forget is there.' Then Asha asks what the platform is for.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Why can't everyone see everything?" Marcus: "Some things are private, like your diary, so only people who really need them get the key."

modules.logline: Running the merged platform as a product puts Marcus and Viktor side by side on service levels, cost and adoption, until Asha must choose one of them to lead it.
scenes: Asha merges both teams into one data platform and gives Marcus and Viktor a quarter to prove it is worth funding. Tomas asks what the platform team actually does. Neither has a crisp answer. Who are its users, really?

Marcus proposes SLOs: trips fresh by 6 a.m. on 99.5% of days. Viktor wants 99.9%. Lena asks what happens when the error budget runs out in week two. Does the team stop shipping features, or keep going?

A Snowflake outage hits during the finance close. Lena runs the incident well, but forty teams learn of it from Kofi. Viktor says the fix mattered more than the updates. How should a platform team communicate during an incident?

Mei brings the bill: the merged platform costs more than both did apart, and nobody knows which team spends what. She wants showback by Friday. Viktor fears it starts a turf war. What is the right unit cost for a trip?

Viktor shows active users rising. Marcus shows time to a trusted number falling from five days to one. Tomas brings fourteen roadmap requests and wants all of them. Which metric shows outcomes, and how do they say no?

Asha asks for one page each: how the platform team should be funded, shaped and staffed for two years. Marcus and Viktor draft separately, then compare. The pages are nearly identical. So why must Asha still pick one?
teasers: Marcus and Viktor argue 99.5% against 99.9%, and an error budget runs out.
Snowflake goes down during the finance close, and forty teams hear it from Kofi.
Mei wants cost showback by Friday, and Viktor fears a turf war.
Tomas brings fourteen roadmap requests and expects every one of them shipped.
Asha asks Marcus and Viktor for one page each on the platform's future.
Asha announces her choice, and Marcus starts writing a strategy both teams can sign.
modules.boss: The weekend review: Asha's quarterly platform review. Present the SLOs and error budget, the incident communication, Mei's unit cost per trip and the adoption numbers that matter. Then defend the three roadmap items you said no to.
modules.finale: The quarter closes: SLOs met, costs shown per team, adoption real. Grace says, 'The job goes to whoever makes the other one better.' Asha calls Marcus and Viktor in together. She has chosen one head of data platform.
modules.zoe: Zoe: "Is the platform a shop?" Marcus: "Sort of; our customers are the other teams, and we only win if they want to come back."
